The pipeline has three stages: Publisher (pub) — reads CSV files from disk, renames columns, and writes to the persons table. Transformer (tfr) — reads persons, filters rows by language, and writes three output tables. Tables — spanish, french, and german each hold the filtered rows for subscribers to consume. The dashed blue line between persons → tfr represents a data-dependency edge: the transformer triggers automatically whenever persons is updated.

First Create a Collection The local-file publisher reads files from a host filesystem path into Tabsdata. It is structurally the same as the cloud file connectors, but the connection is just an absolute base_path with no remote credentials. 1Configure Connection Template→2Create Collection→3Configure Publisher→4Trigger Publisher Point the collection at an absolute local filesystem root. Step 1aGenerate a connection template tdk connection template --type local-file-in --file conn-local.yaml ↓ set the absolute base path conn-local.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.localfile:LocalFileSrcConn spec: base_path: '/data/hr'
connection.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.localfile:LocalFileSrcConn spec: base_path: '/data/hr' base_path:strrequired

Local-file publishers can run on a schedule or in response to another Tabsdata table. Use the mode that best matches how files land on disk. 1Cron2Table Commit Runs on a schedule Use CronTrigger when a watched directory should be polled on a fixed cadence for new files. read_invoices.pyCron from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec, CronTrigger from tabsdatak.conn.localfile import LocalFileSrc @publisher( source=LocalFileSrc( paths=["landing/invoices_*.parquet"], initial_last_modified="2026-01-01T00:00:00Z", ), output_tables=["invoices"], trigger_by=CronTrigger("0 * * * *"), ) def read_invoices( invoices: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: return (invoices[0],)

Use relative paths in LocalFileSrc(paths=[...]); they are resolved under base_path. Wildcards, format detection, initial_last_modified, and file_info behave like the cloud file connectors. In practice: Keep base_path pointed at the stable root for the collection. Use wildcard paths for rolling directories where many similarly named files appear over time. Prefer file_info="name" or file_info="uri" when the downstream pipeline needs to know which file produced each row.

Combine rows from two or more Tabsdata Tables. A transformer declares one input_tables entry per table and takes a parameter for each.

concat() stacks TableFrames by appending their rows. how decides what happens when the inputs do not line up: verticalvertical_relaxeddiagonaldiagonal_relaxed The default, so it can be left off. Every input must share the same columns and the same types. concat.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat @transformer( input_tables=["sales_east", "sales_west"], output_tables=["sales_all"], ) def transform(east: TableFrameSpec, west: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = concat([east, west]) return result sales_east region month amount east jan 10 east feb 20 2 rows sales_west region month amount west jan 30 west feb 40 2 rows sales_all region month amount east jan 10 east feb 20 west jan 30 west feb 40 4 rows note None entries in the list are skipped. A list that is None, empty, or empty once the None entries are dropped makes concat() return None, which leaves the output table on its current version instead of committing a new one. See concat for the full signature.
While TableFrames are typically received as input in publishers and transformers, you can also create them programmatically for testing or data generation purposes.

Use TableFrame.from_dict() to create a TableFrame from a Python dictionary: transform.py from tabsdatak.tableframe import TableFrame data = { "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"], "age": [25, 30, 35], "city": ["New York", "London", "Paris"] } tf = TableFrame.from_dict(data)

Convert a Pandas DataFrame to a TableFrame: transform.py import pandas as pd from tabsdatak.tableframe import TableFrame df = pd.DataFrame({ "product": ["Widget", "Gadget"], "price": [19.99, 29.99] }) tf = TableFrame.from_pandas(df)

Convert from Polars LazyFrame or DataFrame: transform.py import polars as pl from tabsdatak.tableframe import TableFrame # From Polars LazyFrame lf = pl.LazyFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3], "y": [4, 5, 6]}) tf = TableFrame.from_polars(lf) # From Polars DataFrame pdf = pl.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3], "y": [4, 5, 6]}) tf = TableFrame.from_polars(pdf)

Export TableFrames to other formats: transform.py # To dictionary data_dict = tf.to_dict() # To Pandas DataFrame pandas_df = tf.to_pandas() # To Polars DataFrame polars_df = tf.to_polars_df() # To Polars LazyFrame polars_lf = tf.to_polars_lf() See TableFrame API Guide for the whole API in one place.

A transformer reads one or more Tabsdata Tables and writes new Tabsdata Tables. Joining two of them is the most common case: declare both under input_tables and the function takes a parameter for each. See Transformers for the anatomy of a transformer Function. Every block below joins the same two tables. orders has three rows and customers has three, overlapping on two customer_id values: o3 points at c9, which no customer has, and c3 has no order. What a join does with those two rows is the whole difference between the types.

Set the type with how. Every one of these joins on customer_id: innerleftrightfullsemianti Only the rows that match on both sides. The default. join.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["orders", "customers"], output_tables=["order_names"], ) def transform(orders: TableFrameSpec, customers: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = orders.join(customers, on="customer_id") return result orders order_id customer_id amount o1 c1 10 o2 c2 20 o3 c9 5 3 rows customers customer_id name c1 Ada c2 Grace c3 Cy 3 rows order_names order_id customer_id amount name o1 c1 10 Ada o2 c2 20 Grace 2 rows

A key can span several columns, and the two sides can name them differently: on=[...]left_on / right_on One key spanning several columns. A row matches only when every column agrees. join.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["visits", "targets"], output_tables=["visits_vs_target"], ) def transform(visits: TableFrameSpec, targets: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = visits.join(targets, on=["customer_id", "date"]) return result visits customer_id date spend c1 mon 10 c2 mon 7 c1 tue 4 3 rows targets customer_id date target c1 mon 12 c2 mon 5 2 rows visits_vs_target customer_id date spend target c1 mon 10 12 c2 mon 7 5 2 rows

When both tables carry a column of the same name, the right-hand one needs a new name: Renames the right-hand copy of every colliding column. The join key stays single. join.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["orders", "returns"], output_tables=["orders_returns"], ) def transform(orders: TableFrameSpec, returns: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = orders.join(returns, on="id", suffix="_return") return result orders id amount o1 10 o2 20 2 rows returns id amount o1 4 o2 20 2 rows orders_returns id amount amount_return o1 10 4 o2 20 20 2 rows See TableFrame API Guide for the whole API in one place.

Use with_columns() to add new columns or modify existing ones without dropping other columns: Add new columns, or replace exisitng ones. with_columns.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col, lit @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.with_columns( # Add a new calculated column (col("price") * col("quantity")).alias("total"), # Modify an existing column col("name").str.to_uppercase().alias("name"), # Add a literal value column lit("USD").alias("currency") ) return result orders name price quantity widget 10 3 gadget 4 2 2 rows result name price quantity total currency WIDGET 10 3 30 USD GADGET 4 2 8 USD 2 rows

Use rename() to change column names: Give columns new names, leaving their values untouched. rename.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.rename({ "old_name": "new_name", "customer_id": "cust_id" }) return result records old_name customer_id Ada c1 Grace c2 2 rows result new_name cust_id Ada c1 Grace c2 2 rows

Use alias() on expressions to name computed columns: Keep only the listed expressions, in the order given. select.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.select( (col("first_name") + " " + col("last_name")).alias("full_name"), (col("price") * 1.1).alias("price_with_tax") ) return result orders first_name last_name price Ada Lovelace 10 Grace Hopper 20 2 rows result full_name price_with_tax Ada Lovelace 11 Grace Hopper 22 2 rows

Create constant value columns: Add literal value columns with_columns.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import lit @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: result = tf.with_columns( lit(1).alias("version"), lit("active").alias("status"), lit(True).alias("is_valid"), lit(3.14159).alias("pi") ) return result records id 1 2 2 rows result id version status is_valid pi 1 1 active true 3.14159 2 1 active true 3.14159 2 rows See TableFrame API Guide for the whole API in one place.
The .str namespace provides comprehensive string manipulation functions.

to_uppercase()to_lowercase()to_titlecase() Upper-case every character. to_uppercase.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: expr = col("name").str.to_uppercase() return tf.with_columns(expr) persons name age ada Lovelace 36 Grace HOPPER 45 2 rows result name age ADA LOVELACE 36 GRACE HOPPER 45 2 rows

extract()replace()replace_all()replace_many() Extract using regex groups extract.pyOperationFunction from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["source"], output_tables=["result"], ) def transform(tf: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: expr = col("email").str.extract(r"@(\w+)\.", group_index=1) return tf.with_columns(expr) contacts email ada@example.com bo@other.org 2 rows result email example other 2 rows
